---
title: "P-value calibration"
subtitle: "One closed form, and why it restores uniformity"
---

## The calibrated p-value

The [empirical null](null-distribution.qmd) says that under the null hypothesis,
an estimate from this study design is distributed as

$$
\hat\beta \;\sim\; N\!\left(\mu,\ \sigma^2 + \hat\sigma^2\right).
$$

A p-value is the probability, under the null, of an estimate at least as extreme
as the one observed. So substitute that null for the theoretical one and read
off the tail probability. For a new estimate $\hat\beta$ with standard error
$\hat\sigma$:

::: {.keyresult}
$$
p_{\text{upper}} \;=\; \Phi\!\left(\frac{\mu - \hat\beta}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \hat\sigma^2}}\right),
\qquad
p_{\text{lower}} \;=\; \Phi\!\left(\frac{\hat\beta - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \hat\sigma^2}}\right),
$$
$$
p_{\text{two-sided}} \;=\; 2\,\min\!\left(p_{\text{upper}},\, p_{\text{lower}}\right).
$$
:::

No simulation, no iteration — it is one call to the normal CDF. `calibrateP`
computes exactly this, and returns `nan` for any input with a missing or
infinite `logRr` or `seLogRr`.

Setting $\mu = 0$ and $\sigma = 0$ recovers the traditional p-value
$2\Phi(-\lvert\hat\beta\rvert / \hat\sigma)$, which is a useful sanity check and
a real special case: a design with no measurable systematic error is calibrated
to itself.

```{python}
import empiricalcalibration as ec

null_degenerate = ec.Null(0, 0)
print("calibrated under a degenerate null:",
      ec.calibrateP(null_degenerate, 0.2, 0.2)[0])
print("traditional:                      ",
      ec.computeTraditionalP(0.2, 0.2))
```

## Why this restores uniformity

The property a p-value must have is that it is **uniform on $[0,1]$ when the
null hypothesis is true**. That is what makes "reject below 0.05" a test with a
5% type I error rate. The traditional p-value loses this property in the
presence of systematic error; the calibrated one recovers it, and the argument
is two lines.

Take a hypothesis for which the null is true, drawn from the same population of
hypotheses as the controls. By assumption its systematic error is
$\epsilon \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, so

$$
\hat\beta \;\sim\; N\!\left(\mu,\ \sigma^2 + \hat\sigma^2\right)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
Z \;=\; \frac{\hat\beta - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \hat\sigma^2}} \;\sim\; N(0,1).
$$

The calibrated one-sided p-value is $\Phi(-Z)$ — a continuous CDF applied to its
own random variable — and by the probability integral transform that is exactly
$\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$. The two-sided version is uniform by the same argument
applied to $\lvert Z \rvert$.

So calibration is not a heuristic adjustment. Given the model, uniformity under
the null is a theorem. What is *not* guaranteed is the model: the assumption
doing the work is that the hypothesis of interest draws its systematic error
from the same distribution as the controls, and $(\mu, \sigma)$ are estimated
from a finite sample of them.

### Seeing it

Leave each negative control out, calibrate it against a null fitted on the
others, and the resulting p-values should be uniform — so their empirical CDF
should track the diagonal.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Empirical CDF of p-values for negative controls, leave-one-out. Uniform p-values track the diagonal."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import empiricalcalibration as ec

sccs = ec.datasets.sccs()
neg = sccs[sccs.groundTruth == 0].reset_index(drop=True)

trad, calib = [], []
for i in range(len(neg)):
    others = neg.drop(index=i)
    fit = ec.fitNull(others.logRr, others.seLogRr)
    calib.append(ec.calibrateP(fit, neg.logRr[i], neg.seLogRr[i])[0])
    trad.append(ec.computeTraditionalP(neg.logRr[i], neg.seLogRr[i]))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4.6))
grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
for vals, label, colour in [(trad, "traditional", "crimson"),
                            (calib, "calibrated", "#1f4e79")]:
    ax.step(grid, [np.mean(np.asarray(vals) <= g) for g in grid],
            where="post", label=label, color=colour, lw=2)
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], ls="--", color="grey", lw=1, label="uniform")
ax.set_xlabel("p-value"); ax.set_ylabel("fraction of negative controls below")
ax.legend(frameon=False); ax.set_aspect("equal")
fig.tight_layout()
```

```{python}
for name, vals in [("traditional", trad), ("calibrated", calib)]:
    print(f"{name:>12}: {np.mean(np.asarray(vals) < 0.05):.0%} below 0.05 "
          f"(should be 5%)")
```

The traditional curve leaves the diagonal immediately — far too many controls
get small p-values. The calibrated curve is close to uniform, which is the
guarantee restored.

::: {.callout-important}
## Leave-one-out is not optional here

If you fit the null on all the controls and then calibrate those same controls
against it, the p-values will look beautifully uniform whatever the truth is —
the null was fitted to make them so. Any honest check of calibration must hold
out the control being evaluated, which is what the loop above does and what
[`evaluateCiCalibration`](confidence-intervals.qmd#evaluating-coverage) does for
intervals.
:::

## Type 1 error across the null

The fitted null also lets you say, before seeing any result, what the design's
real type I error rate is at a nominal threshold — as a function of how
precisely the outcome is estimated.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Probability of a nominally significant result when the null is true, as a function of standard error, under this study's empirical null."
null = ec.fitNull(neg.logRr, neg.seLogRr)
fig = ec.plotExpectedType1Error(neg.logRr, neg.seLogRr, null=null, alpha=0.05)
```

Precise estimates (small standard error) are *more* likely to be false
positives, not less: as $\hat\sigma \to 0$ the random error disappears but the
systematic error $\sigma$ does not, and the traditional test compares an
estimate centred at $\mu$ against a null centred at 0 with a vanishing yardstick.
That is the "large observational studies are reliably significant" problem in
one figure.

## The MCMC variant

`calibrateP` also accepts an `McmcNull`, in which case the calibration is
performed once per posterior draw and returned with a credible interval:

```{python}
ec.set_seed(123)
mcmc_null = ec.fitMcmcNull(neg.logRr, neg.seLogRr, iter=10_000)
pos = sccs[sccs.groundTruth == 1]
ec.calibrateP(mcmc_null, pos.logRr, pos.seLogRr)
```

The interval reflects uncertainty in $\mu$ and $\sigma$ — the thing the
point-estimate version silently ignores. See [MCMC](mcmc.qmd).

## API

| Function | Returns |
|---|---|
| [`calibrateP(null, logRr, seLogRr, twoSided=True, upper=True)`](../reference/index.qmd#calibratep) | array of calibrated p-values, or a data frame with a credible interval for an `McmcNull` |
| [`computeTraditionalP(logRr, seLogRr, twoSided=True, upper=True)`](../reference/index.qmd#computetraditionalp) | the uncalibrated p-value, for comparison |
| [`plotCalibrationEffect(...)`](../reference/index.qmd#plotcalibrationeffect) | the null band against the theoretical one |
| [`plotExpectedType1Error(...)`](../reference/index.qmd#plotexpectedtype1error) | type I error against standard error |
